candidates.name: ExtendedGapBarStreakPredictsEmaTouch
candidates.quote: if you tested back over the past 10 or 20 years, you would find that more than 95 percent of the time when there were 30 or more consecutive gap bars, the market came back and touched the moving average within 10 bars.
candidates.description: After an extended streak of consecutive same-side moving-average gap bars (about 30 or more, well beyond the ordinary 20-bar 'strong trend' threshold), expect the market to touch the moving average again within about 10 bars; usable as a countertrend fade entry on a marginal new extreme, or as a profit-taking cue for an existing with-trend position.
candidates.pseudocode: consecutiveGapBars(direction) >= extremeGapBarStreak && close[0] > high[1] -> enter countertrend short at next bar's open, expecting a touch of ema[0] within touchWindowBars
candidates.book_order_type: buy/sell the option (or, mechanized here, enter the underlying) on a stop one tick beyond the prior bar's extreme, mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open

complexity.reason: builds on a persistent moving-average-gap-bar streak counter and adds a forward-looking timing window and probability claim, both of which need a separate lookback to instantiate as a coded rule

This chapter is 'Options' and is almost entirely about option mechanics (spreads, premium decay, implied volatility, open interest, skew, earnings catalysts) that the engine has no data for; only a handful of bar-based ideas are recorded here as candidates, and the bulk of the chapter is grouped into a few brief rejected entries below rather than itemized line by line.

candidates.name: FadeStairsPatternBreakout
candidates.quote: When a market is in a stairs pattern, you can fade each new breakout with options, expecting a pullback into the prior stair.
candidates.description: When a trend is advancing in a 'stairs' pattern (a series of small breakouts, each followed by a shallow pullback that stays roughly at or above/below the prior step), fade each new marginal breakout, expecting a pullback back into the prior stair rather than sustained follow-through.
candidates.pseudocode: isStairsPattern(trendDirection) && close[0] > priorStairHigh -> fade entry short, target = priorStairLevel
candidates.book_order_type: enter on a limit at the breakout extreme, or on the close of a weak signal bar (per the book's example); mechanized here as a fade entered at the next bar's open once the breakout+weak-bar condition is true

complexity.reason: identifying a 'stairs pattern' -- a trend of small, roughly-equal steps, distinct from an accelerating spike-and-channel or a three-push wedge -- is a design decision before this could be coded, not just a computation

candidates.name: FadeWeakLow2AtTradingRangeBottom
candidates.quote: A low 2 short signal at the bottom of a trading range usually fails and leads to a reversal up, as do most attempts to break out of a trading range.
candidates.description: A low-2 short setup that forms at the bottom of an established trading range usually fails; treat it as a reversal-up (fade) buying opportunity instead of taking the short. Mirror: a high-2 long setup at the top of a trading range usually fails and is a fade-short opportunity.
candidates.pseudocode: isTradingRange && low2ShortSetupTrue(0) && (close[0] - rangeLow) / (rangeHigh - rangeLow) <= nearRangeFraction -> fade long instead of the short
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (a fade entry gated by range position and an opposing counting setup)

chapter_summary: Chapter 23 is about using options (calls, puts, spreads, risk reversals, cashless collars, delta-neutral hedges) instead of the underlying instrument, and is overwhelmingly about option mechanics the engine has no data for: bid-ask spreads, time decay, implied volatility and skew, open interest, earnings-catalyst premium behavior, and broker execution risk. As expected for this chapter, almost everything is rejected; the few genuinely new bar-level ideas recorded here are an extended (30-bar) moving-average-gap-bar-streak mean-reversion forecast (building on the existing 20-bar streak primitive), a 'stairs pattern' breakout-fade concept, and fading a weak low-2/high-2 counting setup at a trading-range boundary. Everything else -- the chapter's own worked-example charts (AAPL, FCX, Morgan Stanley, SPY, ANR, the Dow's September 2008 flash-crash day) -- narrates already-mined bar-pattern vocabulary (two-legged pullbacks, wedges, moving-average gap bars, double tops, low2/high2, trend-line breaks) purely as a backdrop for which option strategy to use, and was not re-recorded.
